procedural_history.impugned_order: Order passed by the High Court (details in Paragraph 45)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Criminal Appeals were filed in the High Court (details in Paragraph 29). The High Court passed an order (details in Paragraph 45).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: CBI filed Criminal Appeals Nos. 605-616 of 2010 in the Supreme Court. Criminal Appeal Nos. 600-602 of 2010 were before the Supreme Court, which led to the Review Petitions. Sushi I Ansal and Gopal Ansal argued against the review, stating there was no patent error and the review was essentially an appeal in disguise. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the Review Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 712-714 of 2015 and Review Petitions (Criminal) Nos. 770-773 of 2015.

issue.issue_text: Whether there is any merit in the Review Petitions.

facts: The review was sought on the grounds that once the Court decided a sentence needed to be enhanced, it could not then be reduced upon payment of a fine.

The opposing counsel argued that there was no patent error to justify a review, that the arguments had already been considered by the court, and that a review petition cannot be treated as an appeal in disguise.
law: A review petition cannot be treated as an appeal in disguise.
The mere possibility of two different views on an issue is not a sufficient ground for a review.
To invoke review jurisdiction, there must be a patent error in the original judgment.
application: The Court gave "deep consideration to the rival submissions" from both parties.
The Court considered the arguments presented by the petitioners for the review.
The Court also considered the counter-arguments that the threshold for a review, such as a patent error, had not been met and that the issues had already been argued.
reasoning.conclusion: After considering the arguments from both sides, the Supreme Court found that there was no merit in the Review Petitions and consequently dismissed them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there is any merit in the Review Petitions.
appellant_arguments: The default sentence cannot exceed ¼ of the term of imprisonment prescribed for the offence.
respondent_arguments: The sentence awarded is not illegal or unjustified, as relief can be moulded in individual cases based on the specific facts.
Showing undue sympathy by imposing an inadequate sentence could lead to a miscarriage of justice.
An adequate sentence is required to create an element of fear in the mind of the offender.
The sentence prescribed under Section 304-A IPC should be revisited by lawmakers.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court must limit itself to the sentencing choices available under the law prescribing the sentence for the specific offense.
obiter: A default sentence cannot exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment prescribed for the offence.
Relief can be moulded in individual cases having regard to the fact situation.
A matter of this magnitude may call for a higher sentence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court's original order, viewed as a whole, appropriately balanced the interests of justice by imposing a substantial fine to be used for a public purpose—setting up or upgrading trauma centers—in lieu of an enhanced prison sentence, and there is neither any illegality nor any impropriety in this decision that would warrant a review.
legal_tests_applied: The review petition cannot be treated as an appeal in disguise.
Mere possibility of two views cannot be a ground for review.

The sentence has to be awarded in the light of nature of offence, prescribed sentence, over all fact situation, mitigating and aggravating circumstances, including age of the offender, his background, possibility of return to normal 1 ife and need of the society.

Having regard to the wide discretion available to the court under Section 304 A, and having regard to the fact that the High Court and this Court, in appeal, had limited the imprisonment to one year, in our view, the punishment which would serve deterrence and public purpose by both imprisonment and exemplary fine, would be an appropriate punishment.
why_appellant_lost: There is no patent error which may justify invocation of review jurisdiction.
The arguments now sought to be raised were before the Court when the order was passed by this Court.
why_respondent_won: The Court's order must be seen as a whole and cannot be split into different sentences; the operative part shows the Court tried to balance the interest of justice by imposing a substantial fine in lieu of an additional period of enhanced sentence.
Imposition of expiatory fine in addition to incarceration would also serve the penalogical purpose of deterrence having regard also to recidivism.
In larger public interest, the view taken by Gyan Sudha Misra, J. [to recover a large amount by way of fine to be used for the trauma centre] was the underlying idea in enhancing the punishment.
policy_considerations: The fine was to be utilized for setting up of or upgrading the trauma centres of the Delhi Government hospitals.
The punishment which would serve deterrence and public purpose by both imprisonment and exemplary fine, would be an appropriate punishment.
There should be element of fear in the mind of offender for which adequate sentence was required to be imposed.
